title: Nonparametric In-Context Learning under Growing Geometric Complexity: Minimax Optimality and Local Geometry-Adaptivity of Transformers
claim: Data lie on a mixture of heterogeneous manifolds with differing dimensions and noise levels, observed through perturbed covariates.
layout: 3 shapes side by side with ellipsis, left-to-right, shaded noise neighborhoods
description: A horizontal row of three geometric objects separated by an ellipsis. On the left is a closed curve drawn in blue-gray, in the middle is an ellipsoidal surface in tan or brown with dashed hidden contours, and on the right is a torus in olive-green. The ellipsis between the ellipsoid and the torus marks omitted components. Each object sits inside a pale, wider shaded halo of the same hue, which shows its component-specific noise bound. Small filled dots sit on each manifold as latent covariates. Each is paired with a nearby open circle, the observed noisy covariate, and a short segment joins the two to show the perturbation. The eye goes first to the colorful shapes and the dot pairs. The figure has no text or math labels. It is a clean, schematic setup illustration.
caption: A heterogeneous manifold mixture with bounded covariate noise. The closed curve, ellipsoidal surface, and torus represent components of intrinsic dimensions one, two, and two, respectively; the ellipsis denotes omitted components. Filled dots mark latent covariates $X_i^\star$ on the manifolds, and open circles mark observed covariates $X_i=X_i^\star+\xi_i$. The connecting segments indicate the perturbations $\xi_i$, while the pale shaded neighborhoods schematically depict component-specific noise bounds $\|\xi_i\|\le \sigma_{k,n}$. In the growing-complexity setting, the number of components $K_n$ may increase while the reach and separation lower bounds $\tau_{0,n}$ and $\delta_{0,n}$ may decrease with $n$.
abstract: Transformers have become a central architecture for in-context learning (ICL), particularly through their state-of-the-art performance in large language models. This success motivates understanding how transformers exploit intrinsic geometry of real-world data. However, existing nonparametric ICL theory has largely focused on simplified settings, such as Euclidean domains or single manifold models, failing to fully explain its phenomenal empirical success in complex tasks. To address this gap, we study the prediction problem under unknown heterogeneous geometry, modeled by sample size-dependent mixtures of manifolds with heterogeneous dimensions, smoothness, and sampling masses. Under the growing geometric complexity model, we establish a minimax lower bound capturing the aggregate difficulty of the components and construct an oracle tangent local polynomial estimator with a matching upper bound. This estimator is connected to a structure-informed, two-stage softmax transformer with a geometric preconditioner and local polynomial solvers. The transformer achieves negligible approximation error relative to the minimax rate with logarithmic depth and polynomial size. Finally, we derive an in-context generalization bound for near empirical risk minimizers (ERM) over this class. Together, these results identify conditions under which the resulting predictor exploits local geometry and attains minimax rate.
